To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of vertical transmission of HIV is reduced by the administration of antiretroviral therapy (ART) to pregnant women and to the newborns.

the risk of transmission of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) from mother to fetus is 15-20% and is higher in women with a low CD4+ T-cell count and in those with high plasma HIV-1 RNA load.

the maternal-fetal transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is not an inevitable event, and that the use of antiretrovirals during pregnancy and the perinatal period can prevent this transmission.

The main takeaway from our work is that
maternal-fetal transmission of HIV can occur in the first trimester of gestation.
the transmission of HIV-1 to the fetus is possible in the absence of a detectable viral load in the mother's serum, as well as in the absence of detectable HIV-1 RNA in the cervicovaginal secretions.
maternal-fetal transmission of HIV-1 is not only possible, but also quite common in our setting, where the rate of transmission is 25.8%.
